stories.title: Singapore's First Cyber Guard Warns: AI Hackers Are Getting Smarter
stories.headline_kid: The man who built Singapore's cyber defence force says computer attacks are changing fast because of AI, and we need new ways to stay safe.
summary: Mr David Koh was the very first boss of the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA), the government team that protects our country's important computer systems, like banks, hospitals and power supplies. He recently retired after leading CSA since it started, and in his first big interview since stepping down, he shared what worries him most.

Mr Koh explained that hackers (people who break into computers to steal information or cause trouble) are now using Artificial Intelligence, or AI, to attack faster and smarter than before. Think of it like burglars who used to pick locks slowly by hand, but now have a super-fast robot tool that can crack any lock in seconds.

Because AI attacks happen so quickly, Mr Koh says Singapore cannot defend itself the old way anymore, where humans slowly check for problems one by one. Instead, Singapore needs its own smart AI tools to spot danger instantly and fight back.
This matters to everyone, not just big companies. Scams, fake messages and stolen passwords can happen to ordinary families too, so staying alert online is now more important than ever.

lenses.me: If you play online games or use apps, this is why you should never share your passwords, even with 'friends' online.
lenses.family: Your parents' online banking and shopping apps are protected by teams like CSA working hard behind the scenes.
lenses.friends: You and your classmates can talk about spotting scam messages, like fake prize alerts or strange links.
lenses.nation: Singapore is building smarter digital defences so our hospitals, transport and banks stay safe from attacks.
lenses.world: Countries everywhere are racing to use AI for both attacking and defending computer systems, making cybersecurity a global challenge.

stories.title: North Korean Leader's Sister Slams Singapore's Neighbours Over Nuclear Weapons
stories.headline_kid: The powerful sister of North Korea's leader got angry at ASEAN, the group of countries Singapore belongs to, for asking North Korea to give up its dangerous weapons.
summary: Kim Yo Jong is the sister of Kim Jong Un, the leader of North Korea, and she is one of the most powerful people in the country. On Monday, she strongly criticised ASEAN, calling its stance 'stupid and foolish'.

ASEAN stands for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, a group of 10 countries in our region, including Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand, that work together on peace and trade. Last week, at ASEAN's yearly meeting, the group expressed 'grave concern', which means they were very worried, about North Korea's nuclear weapons programme.

Nuclear weapons are extremely powerful and dangerous bombs that can cause massive destruction. When countries ask North Korea to 'denuclearise', they mean asking it to give up these weapons completely, to keep the region safer.

Kim Yo Jong's angry response shows that North Korea has no plans to give up its weapons anytime soon, which keeps tensions high in Asia, even though this conflict is happening far from Singapore's shores.

lenses.me: You'll hear the word 'ASEAN' often in school - it's the group of neighbouring countries Singapore works with for peace and trade.
lenses.family: Your family may discuss news like this at home, especially if relatives travel to countries near this region.
lenses.friends: You and your friends might discuss in Social Studies class how countries in a region cooperate, like ASEAN does.
lenses.nation: As an ASEAN member, Singapore supports peaceful solutions and safety in our region, even when other countries disagree.
lenses.world: Nuclear tensions between North Korea and other nations affect global safety discussions, even in faraway places.

compo_words.meaning: to remove or give up nuclear weapons

compo_words.meaning: a feeling of unease or conflict between groups

stories.title: Typhoon Noul's Rain Spreads Floods Across Southern China
stories.headline_kid: After crashing into land, Typhoon Noul is now dumping so much rain that seven regions in China are bracing for flash floods.
summary: Remember Typhoon Noul, which hit southern China over the weekend? It's not over yet. After making landfall, the storm is now bringing heavy to torrential rain, which means extremely heavy rainfall, across a huge stretch of southern China.

Authorities have warned that flash floods, which are sudden and fast-rising floods, are expected in seven areas: Jiangxi, Hunan, Guangdong, Sichuan, Shaanxi, Gansu and southeastern Xinjiang. That's a much bigger area than just the coast where the typhoon first landed.
The storm's gale-force winds already caused flight cancellations at Hong Kong's international airport, and cleaners have been busy clearing fallen branches and leaves from the streets in Shenzhen.
If your family has travel plans to Hong Kong or southern China soon, it's worth checking flight and weather updates, as more rain and possible delays could be on the way.

lenses.me: If you're travelling to China or Hong Kong soon, your flight schedule might be affected by this weather.
lenses.family: Families with travel plans should check flight status updates before heading to the airport.
lenses.friends: You could discuss with classmates how typhoons form and why they cause so much rain.
lenses.nation: Singapore Airlines and other airlines flying to affected regions may need to adjust schedules.
lenses.world: Extreme weather events like typhoons are becoming a bigger concern as climate patterns shift globally.

compo_words.meaning: to move people away from a dangerous place to safety

stories.title: F1 Returns to Malaysia in October - Right Before Singapore's Big Race!
stories.headline_kid: Formula One racing cars are coming back to Malaysia's Sepang circuit this October, just one week before the exciting Singapore Grand Prix!
summary: Formula One, often called F1, is one of the fastest and most exciting motorsports in the world, where drivers race specially-built cars around a track at incredible speeds. F1 announced that Malaysia's Sepang circuit, near Kuala Lumpur's airport, will host a race in October.
This race is actually a rescheduled Bahrain Grand Prix, meaning the race originally planned for Bahrain (a country in the Middle East) will now happen in Malaysia instead, on October 4.

This Malaysia race fits neatly into F1's busy calendar, coming after the Azerbaijan Grand Prix on September 26, and right before our very own Singapore Grand Prix on October 11. That means racing fans in this region get three big races close together!

For Singapore, this is exciting news because fans who love watching F1 live might travel to Malaysia to catch the action before heading home to watch the Singapore race, held on our famous night street circuit.

lenses.me: If you enjoy watching fast cars, you might get to see two exciting F1 races close together this year!
lenses.family: Your family might plan a trip to catch the Malaysia race, or watch the Singapore Grand Prix together.
lenses.friends: You and your friends can chat about which F1 drivers you're rooting for this season.
lenses.nation: Singapore's own night race in October will benefit from the buzz building up in the region.
lenses.world: F1 races bring together fans and drivers from all over the world, showing how sports connect countries.

stories.title: Small Kind Acts That Make Singapore a Better Place
stories.headline_kid: Two university experts say that little everyday choices, like moving into the train or giving way to others, quietly shape what kind of country Singapore becomes.
summary: Have you ever squeezed onto a crowded MRT train and wondered why some passengers won't move further into the carriage? Two writers from the Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS) wrote about how these small daily moments matter more than we think.

They explain that it's not just big government policies that shape Singapore's society. It's also the tiny, repeated choices we make every day, like giving up a seat, moving in to let others board, or waiting patiently instead of pushing ahead.

The writers point to real examples, like MRT posters reminding commuters not to groom themselves (like clipping nails or applying makeup) in public, showing that everyday courtesy needs gentle reminders sometimes.
The main idea is simple: being kind and thoughtful in small ways, again and again, slowly builds the kind of caring, gracious Singapore we all want to live in.

lenses.me: Next time you're on the MRT or bus, think about moving in or giving up your seat - small actions really do matter!
lenses.family: Your family can talk about small acts of kindness you can do together in public spaces.
lenses.friends: You and your friends could try being extra considerate to classmates, like sharing space or waiting your turn.
lenses.nation: Singapore's identity as a gracious society depends on everyone doing their small part, not just the government.
lenses.world: Many crowded cities around the world face similar challenges of building courtesy and consideration among strangers.

compo_words.example: A gracious society is built through small acts of kindness.

compo_words.meaning: thoughtful about the needs and feelings of others
